SHORT REPORT
A Patient With Atypical Stiff-Person
Syndrome: An Electrophysiological Study
Giuseppe Picciolo, Angelo Quartarone, Fortunato Battaglia, Giovanni Majorana,
Vincenzo Rizzo, Sergio Bagnato, Paolo Girlanda, and Corrado Messina
Abstract
We describe a patient with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus who noticed pain and stiffness in the neck
and painful spasms and rigidity of the right thigh. Continuous motor unit activity was recorded in the lower
limb muscles on the right side and in the cervical paraspinal muscles. Cutaneomuscular reflexes were at an
abnormally low threshold recording from the muscles of the right leg. Laboratory investigation revealed
anti-GAD antibodies in serum and oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid. We conclude that the patient
has atypical stiff-person syndrome.
J Clin Neuromusc Dis 2001;3:20–22. Copyright © 2001 Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, Inc.
The stiff-person syndrome is a rare disorder characterized
by a chronic progressive axial rigidity and superimposed
painful spasms that may be spontaneous or evoked by noise
or fright.
1,2 Occasionally the same clinical features may be
confined to one limb (focal stiff-person syndrome) when
corticobasal degeneration, encephalomyelitis, and focal le-
sions of the spinal cord are excluded.
3
We report on a patient with a chronic progressive dis-
order characterized by continuous motor unit activity
(CMUA), painful involuntary spasms, and stiffness con-
fined to the neck and to the right thigh with no evidence
of cerebral, brainstem, extrapyramidal, pyramidal, or sen-
sory dysfunction. We consider that our patient has atypical
stiff-person syndrome.
Case Report
We describe a 34-year-old patient with insulin-dependent
diabetes mellitus who first noticed pain and stiffness in the
neck 2 years earlier. This was followed later by painful
spasms and rigidity of the right thigh. Voluntary move-
ments, unexpected noises, or sudden emotions induced the
spasms. Thoracolumbar, paraspinal, and abdominal
muscles were not involved. Apart from stiffness, the neu-
rologic examination revealed decrease of the deep tendon
reflexes in the lower limb and an impairment of vibration
sense below the knee.
Laboratory investigations showed antibodies directed
against glutamic acid decarboxylase in serum. An oligo-
clonal pattern of immunoglobulin G was detected in ce-
rebrospinal fluid. Extensive investigation, including the
imaging of the whole neuraxis, failed to disclose any
abnormality.
Our patient was treated with 0.4 mg/kg intravenous
immunoglobulin per day for 5 days during hospitalization
with only a mild improvement.
Subsequently this patient received 10 mg clonazepam
and 50 mg baclofen per day, and 3 months later a clinical
and electrophysiological examination revealed an improve-
ment of clinical symptoms with reduced frequency and
intensity of painful spasms of the right thigh.
Clinical Neurophysiological Studies
Standard Electromyography and Nerve
Conduction Studies
Needle electromyography (EMG) was performed in the
brachial biceps, first dorsal interosseous, quadriceps, and
tibialis anterior muscles on the right side. The analysis of
motor unit potentials demonstrated polyphasic and large
motor unit potentials. A decreased recruitment was also
found.
Routine nerve conduction studies were performed in
ulnar, peroneal, and sural nerves on the right side. The
sural sensory response was absent and the peroneal motor
study showed slowed conduction velocity (Table 1).

All these findings were the result of mild polyneuropathy.
Electromyography Recording of Spontaneous
and Induced Spasms
Study of spontaneous and induced muscle spasms were
also performed. Surface EMG recordings were obtained

apart longitudinally over the muscle bellies. We recorded

muscles on both sides. The results were confirmed by

surface electrodes and then confirmed by needle EMG in
the paraspinal cervical and thigh muscles. Voluntary move-

ment elicits reflex spasms in the lower limb. Moreover, the
spasms could be induced by electrical shocks delivered at
the ankle or by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of
the motor cortex. The latency of the direct response in the
lower limb muscles after TMS was within normal values.
The spasms were induced in tight muscles after TMS and
consisted of co-contracting EMG activity in antagonistic
muscle pairs (quadriceps and hamstring), in the right lower
limb, and lasted several seconds. Spasms have a similar
threshold to the direct response in the same muscle and
begin in quadriceps at approximately 80 msec.
Cutaneomuscular/Exteroceptive Reflexes
Cutaneomuscular/exteroceptive reflexes were elicited after
a single shock delivered to the tibial nerve at the ankle
according to the technique described by Meinck et al.
4,5
Surface EMG recordings were obtained from the gastroc-
nemius, tibialis anterior, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis
muscles on both sides. Cutaneomuscular/exteroceptive re-
flexes were of an abnormally low threshold. Stimulus at
three times the sensory threshold gave consistent short and
long latency responses in tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius,
vastus lateralis, biceps femoris (Fig. 1).
Somatosensory and Motor Evoked Potentials
Somatosensory evoked potentials and motor evoked po-
tentials did not detect any sign of long tract involvement.
The patient gave informed consent to all performed neu-
rophysiological studies.
Discussion
We consider that our patient has a“focal stiff-person syn-
drome.” The most striking clinical feature of our patient
was the presence of painful spasms of the right thigh which
occurred spontaneously or were induced by voluntary ac-
tion or unexpected noises. These spasms were also associ-
ated with stiffness of the neck muscles. Limb dystonia is
unlikely, because dystonic spasms are generally less painful
and not stimulus-sensitive. Spasticity can be excluded, be-
cause there were no upper motor neuron signs and central
motor conduction time was normal. The association of
stimulus-sensitive spasms and CMUA in leg muscles is
seen in several diseases involving the spinal cord. Its long
tract involvement, abnormal cerebrospinal fluid, and cata-
strophic course can easily differentiate idiopathic enceph-
alomyelitis with rigidity. The stiff-person syndrome bears
the closest similarity to the patient presented here. How-
ever, the symptoms of our patient were peculiar. In typical
stiff-person syndrome, the core features are rigidity,
spasms, and CMUA of the trunk muscles, with slow pro-
gression to proximal muscles. In our patient, the proximal
leg muscles were the most affected, with mild involvement
of the cervical paraspinal muscles and leg muscles and spar-
ing of the thoracolumbar and abdominal muscles. On the
other hand, our patient had anti-GAD antibodies in serum
(109 U/mL; radioimmunoassay) and oligoclonal bands in
the cerebrospinal fluid that, even if not pathognomonic,
are widely reported in stiff-person syndrome.
2
There are two stiff-person syndromes with atypical fea-
tures described in the literature, the jerking stiff-person
syndrome
6,7 and the focal stiff-person syndrome.7,8 The
first syndrome is characterized by a brainstem myoclonus
that involves all four limbs. Rigidity and painful spasms of
the limbs characterize the latter, especially distally in the
legs, while the axial muscles are usually spared.
Our patient seems to have a form a focal stiff-person

syndrome even if there is involvement of proximal muscles
and cervical paraspinal muscles. These data suggest that in
“focal stiff-person syndrome” an involvement of proximal
muscles and neck muscles could sometimes occur.
